rw: An income stock pays relatively high, steady dividends, so investors holding it receive regular cash income rather than relying only on price growth over time.

ww.A stock that pays no dividends and reinv: A stock that pays no dividends and reinvests all profit is a growth stock, which is the opposite of an income stock that distributes cash.
ww.A stock issued only by banks and insurer: Income stocks are not defined by issuer type or state; banks and insurers are only some of many companies that happen to pay dividends.
ww.A stock that falls every year by design: Nothing in stock design makes a share fall every year by rule; income stocks are valued for dividends and can rise or fall like others.

rw: A ticker symbol is a short code of letters, such as AAPL, that uniquely identifies a listed company on an exchange so orders reach the right security.

ww.A tax code for corporations and firms: A tax code identifies how a corporation is taxed and has nothing to do with market trading, whereas a ticker symbol identifies a listed company on an exchange.
ww.A government license number for firms: A government license number authorizes a firm to operate, but a ticker is simply an exchange label for a listed security, not any kind of license.
ww.A password to log in to a broker's site: A broker login password protects an account, while a ticker symbol is public and only names the stock, so it cannot be a password.

rw: Regular U.S. stock market sessions run 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern on business days, which is when most exchange trading takes place for ordinary investors.

ww.8:00 p.m. to midnight Eastern, when mark: Eight p.m. to midnight Eastern is after the market has closed, not when it closes, and regular trading does not take place during those hours.
ww.Only on weekends and public holidays eac: Regular trading happens on weekdays and exchanges are closed on weekends and public holidays, so trading only then is the reverse of the real schedule.
ww.24 hours every day of the year, with no: U.S. exchanges do not operate around the clock; regular sessions have a fixed open and close, and markets are shut overnight, on weekends and on holidays.

rw: A circuit breaker pauses trading after a sharp market decline, giving investors time to absorb information and reducing panic selling that could worsen a crash.

ww.A fee charged for large trades made on t: A circuit breaker is not a fee; exchanges do not charge extra for large trades, and the mechanism instead halts trading to calm sharp price drops.
ww.A tax on rapid trades made by day trader: A tax on rapid trades would be a government levy, but a circuit breaker is an exchange rule that temporarily halts trading after large declines.
ww.A device that cuts the electricity to tr: The name borrows from electrical equipment, but a stock exchange circuit breaker does not cut power to traders; it only pauses trading when prices fall sharply.

rw: Short selling means selling borrowed shares first and buying them back later, hopefully at a lower price, so the seller keeps the difference as profit.

ww.Selling shares of a short company name t: Short selling has nothing to do with a short company name; the word "short" refers to owing shares you borrowed and sold, not to the name.
ww.Buying shares for a short time only, not: Buying shares for a short time is just brief ownership and a long position; short selling instead begins with selling borrowed shares you do not own.
ww.Selling shares you own after a long hold: Selling shares you already own after a long hold is an ordinary sale of a long position, not a short sale, which requires borrowing shares.

rw: The seller receives $50 per share and rebuys at $40, gaining $10 per share, so 100 shares times $10 equals a $1,000 gain before any costs.

ww.$4,000: A $4,000 gain would need a $40 drop per share on 100 shares, but the price fell only $10, from $50 to $40, so that is too large.
ww.$5,000: A $5,000 gain would equal selling at $50 times 100 shares, which is the sale proceeds, not the profit; the profit is the $10 drop times 100 shares.
ww.$500: A $500 gain would imply only a $5 drop per share, but the stock fell $10 from $50 to $40, so profit on 100 shares is double that.

rw: Margin trading means borrowing money from a broker to buy securities, using the account's holdings as collateral, which magnifies both gains and losses on the investment.

ww.Trading only with cash on hand and no lo: Trading only with cash and no loans is a cash account; margin trading is the opposite because it uses borrowed money from a broker to buy securities.
ww.Trading only on the edges of a market, n: Margin has nothing to do with trading at market edges; the word refers to the borrowed funds and collateral cushion in an account, not a price location.
ww.Trading in very small share amounts at a: Trading in very small share amounts describes odd lots or fractional trading, which are unrelated to margin, where a broker lends part of the purchase price.

rw: A margin call is the broker's demand for more cash or securities when account value falls below the required level, protecting the loan the broker made.

ww.A tax notice from the IRS about your tra: A margin call comes from the broker, not the IRS, and it concerns account collateral falling short rather than any tax notice about trading gains.
ww.A message that confirms a trade has been: A trade confirmation reports that an order was executed, but a margin call is a demand to add funds because the account equity has fallen too low.
ww.A phone call offering a bonus to new bro: A margin call is not a sales call offering bonuses to new clients; it is a warning that your borrowed account needs more money immediately.

rw: A commodity is a basic raw material, such as oil, wheat or copper, traded in markets where units from different producers are largely interchangeable.

ww.A bank deposit held by a customer: A bank deposit is money held at a bank earning interest, which is a financial product, whereas a commodity is a physical raw material traded in markets.
ww.A loan to a company from a lender: A loan to a company from a lender is a debt arrangement, not a commodity; commodities are raw goods such as oil, wheat or gold.
ww.A share of ownership held by an investor: A share of ownership held by an investor is equity in a company, not a commodity, which is a raw material that is largely interchangeable.

rw: A futures contract is an agreement to buy or sell an asset at a set price on a future date, letting parties lock in prices today.

ww.A share of a company's future profits ea: Receiving a share of future profits each year describes owning stock, not a futures contract, which is an agreement to trade an asset later at a set price.
ww.A promise to pay dividends at a later da: A promise to pay dividends later describes a company's declared dividend, while a futures contract obliges the parties to buy and sell an asset at a fixed price.
ww.A loan repaid at some point in the futur: A loan repaid in the future is a debt, like a bond, whereas a futures contract is an agreement to exchange an asset at a preset price later.

rw: Hedging means taking an offsetting action, such as using options or futures, to reduce the risk of loss from price changes in an existing investment.

ww.Taking a bigger risk to earn a higher pr: Taking a bigger risk hoping for higher profit is speculation, the opposite of hedging, which is meant to reduce rather than increase exposure to price changes.
ww.Planting bushes around a house to make a: Planting bushes is the literal meaning of a garden hedge, but in finance hedging is a risk strategy, not a landscaping task or boundary fence.
ww.Ignoring risk entirely and hoping for th: Ignoring risk and hoping for the best is the opposite of hedging, because hedging deliberately takes steps to protect against adverse price movements instead of ignoring them.

rw: Speculation means accepting high risk hoping for a large profit, usually from short-term price moves, with a real chance of significant loss instead.

ww.Saving money in a bank for the long run: Saving money in a bank for the long run is a low-risk plan aiming for safety and steady interest, which is the opposite of speculation.
ww.Reducing risk by spreading money out wid: Reducing risk by spreading money across many assets is diversification, which lowers risk, whereas speculation concentrates on bets with potentially large gains and losses.
ww.Paying off debt early to cut interest co: Paying off debt early to cut interest costs is a cautious money habit that saves interest, and it is not a high-risk market bet like speculation.

rw: A derivative is a contract whose value depends on another asset, such as a stock, bond, commodity or index, which is called the underlying asset.

ww.A share of ownership in a company with v: A share with voting rights is ownership in a company, which is common stock; a derivative gets its value from another asset rather than being ownership.
ww.A bank account with a fixed rate of inte: A bank account with a fixed interest rate is a deposit product whose value does not depend on an underlying asset, so it is not a derivative.
ww.A government tax rule that applies to fi: A government tax rule that applies to firms is a legal requirement, not a financial instrument, so it cannot be a derivative contract.

rw: The Federal Reserve is the U.S. central bank and sets monetary policy, including targets for interest rates, which influences borrowing costs and financial markets broadly.

ww.It lists new companies for trading on ex: Listing new companies for trading is done by stock exchanges such as the NYSE and Nasdaq, not by the Federal Reserve, which sets monetary policy.
ww.It collects personal income tax from wor: Personal income tax is collected by the Internal Revenue Service, a Treasury agency, not by the Federal Reserve, which manages monetary policy and bank supervision.
ww.It sets the price of each stock by order: Stock prices come from buyers and sellers in the market, not from the Fed, which influences them only indirectly through interest rates and monetary policy.

rw: Higher rates raise borrowing costs for companies and make bonds more attractive, so stocks may fall when the Fed signals increases, though the reaction can vary.

ww.They stop trading for the rest of a week: Markets do not stop trading for a week because of a Fed signal; exchanges close only on set schedules or short circuit breaker halts.
ww.They close for the day or the week: Fed announcements do not close exchanges for a day or week; trading continues and prices simply adjust to the news as investors react.
ww.They always rise right away at once: Stocks do not always rise at once after a rate hike signal; higher rates often pressure stock prices, and the word "always" makes this wrong.

rw: A credit rating is an assessment of a borrower's ability and likelihood to repay debt, which lenders and investors use to judge risk and set rates.

ww.A tax on borrowing by firms and people: A tax on borrowing would be a government levy, but a credit rating is an independent opinion of how likely a borrower is to repay.
ww.A list of a company's customers and orde: A list of customers and orders is a sales record for a business, whereas a credit rating assesses a borrower's ability to repay debt.
ww.A bank's interest rate on all its loans: A bank's interest rate on its loans is a price of borrowing, not a credit rating, which measures the borrower's creditworthiness instead.

rw: AAA is the highest rating, from agencies such as S&P, meaning the issuer is extremely likely to repay, so it carries the lowest default risk.

ww.D: A rating of D means the issuer is already in default, which is the highest possible default risk and the opposite of the safest rating.
ww.CCC: CCC is a very low rating signaling substantial risk of default, so it is far riskier than AAA, which indicates the strongest repayment capacity.
ww.BB: BB is below investment grade, in the speculative or junk category, so it carries notable default risk and is much riskier than top-rated AAA bonds.

rw: A junk bond has a low credit rating, below investment grade, so it pays a higher yield to compensate investors for the greater risk of default.

ww.A bond that cannot be traded on exchange: Junk bonds can be traded on exchanges and over the counter like other bonds, so being untradable does not define them; low credit rating does.
ww.A bond rated AAA by the major rating age: AAA is the top rating, which marks the safest bonds, so a bond rated AAA is the opposite of a junk bond.
ww.A government bond with the lowest risk o: A government bond with the lowest risk of loss, like a Treasury, is the safest kind, whereas junk bonds are speculative and higher risk.

rw: A bond's yield is the return earned expressed as a percent of its price, so it lets investors compare the income from different bonds.

ww.The date the bond is issued to buyers: The date a bond is issued is just its issue date and has no bearing on yield, which measures the annual return relative to price.
ww.The amount a company borrowed from lende: The amount a company borrowed is the bond's principal or face value, not its yield, which expresses return as a percent of price paid.
ww.The fee charged by the broker for the bo: A broker's fee is a transaction cost and does not define yield, which measures the income and return an investor earns as a percent of price.

rw: Bond price and yield move in opposite directions: when prices rise yields fall, and when prices fall yields rise, because coupon payments stay fixed.

ww.They are quite unrelated in price: Price and yield are closely linked by the math of present value, so calling them unrelated is wrong; a change in one changes the other.
ww.They always move the same way: They do not move together; when a bond's price rises, the fixed interest becomes a smaller percent of the higher price, so yield falls.
ww.They are always exactly equal: Price and yield are not always equal; a 5% coupon bond priced at $1,000 yields 5%, but at $900 its yield is higher.

rw: Fundamental analysis judges a company's health and intrinsic value by examining financial statements such as the income statement, balance sheet and cash flows.

ww.Predicting prices by studying past price: Studying past price charts and patterns to predict prices is technical analysis, not fundamental analysis, which focuses on the company's financial health and value.
ww.Choosing stocks by guessing at random ea: Guessing at random each day is not analysis at all; fundamental analysis is a disciplined study of a company's finances and prospects.
ww.Using only news headlines to pick stocks: Relying only on news headlines is a shallow, reactive approach, whereas fundamental analysis examines the financial statements and business quality behind the stock price.

rw: Technical analysis studies price charts and trading volume to spot patterns and forecast future price movements, rather than examining the company's underlying financial statements.

ww.Interviewing managers and reading the an: Interviewing managers and reading the annual report is part of fundamental research on the business, not technical analysis, which studies charts and volume.
ww.Calculating the company's tax bill for t: Calculating a company's tax bill is an accounting task and has no role in technical analysis, which uses price and volume data to forecast.
ww.Reading a company's annual report cover: Reading an annual report cover to cover is fundamental analysis of company disclosures, while technical analysis relies on price charts and trading volume instead.

rw: EPS is net income divided by shares outstanding, which shows how much profit is earned for each share held by investors.

ww.The total assets divided by liabilities: Total assets divided by liabilities is an asset coverage ratio, a measure of solvency, and it does not show profit earned per share.
ww.The share price divided by dividends: Share price divided by dividends is not EPS; EPS uses net income over shares, while price divided by earnings per share gives the P/E ratio.
ww.The revenue divided by employees on payr: Revenue divided by employees measures productivity per worker, not profit per share, so it is unrelated to what EPS measures.

rw: EPS equals net income divided by shares, so $20 million divided by 5 million shares gives $4.00 of earnings for each share.

ww.$15.00: A $15.00 EPS would need $75 million in earnings across 5 million shares, but the company earns $20 million, so this is far too high.
ww.$0.25: An EPS of $0.25 comes from inverting the division, 5 divided by 20, but earnings must be divided by shares, giving $4.00 instead.
ww.$100.00: An EPS of $100.00 would require $500 million in earnings with 5 million shares, which is far above the $20 million this company earns.

rw: The P/E ratio is price divided by earnings per share, showing what investors are paying for each dollar of a company's earnings.

ww.How much a company pays in dividends: Dividends paid are shown by dividend yield or payout, not the P/E ratio, which compares share price with earnings per share.
ww.How many shares a company has issued: The number of shares issued is shown in the share count, not the P/E ratio, which relates price to earnings and not share count.
ww.How much debt a company has on its books: A company's debt load is shown by ratios like debt to equity, not by P/E, which only compares share price with earnings.

rw: P/E equals price divided by earnings per share, so $45 divided by $3 gives 15, meaning investors pay $15 for every $1 of earnings.

ww.42: A P/E of 42 comes from subtracting $3 from $45, but P/E requires division, not subtraction, so this value is incorrect.
ww.135: A P/E of 135 would result from multiplying $45 by $3, but P/E is price divided by earnings, so the correct figure is much smaller.
ww.0.067: A P/E of 0.067 comes from dividing earnings by price, $3 over $45, which inverts the formula and gives the earnings yield, not the P/E.

rw: Dividend yield is annual dividends per share divided by the share price, showing the income return an investor gets from owning the stock.

ww.Debt divided by total equity of a firm: Debt divided by total equity is the debt-to-equity ratio, which measures leverage, not dividend yield, which compares dividends to the share price.
ww.Price divided by earnings, a different r: Price divided by earnings is the P/E ratio, a valuation measure, and is a different calculation from dividend yield, which uses dividends per share.
ww.Profit divided by sales for the year: Profit divided by sales is the profit margin, a measure of operating efficiency, and not dividend yield, which relates payouts to share price.

rw: Dividend yield equals annual dividends divided by price, so $2 divided by $50 equals 0.04, or 4%, the income return on the share price.

ww.2%: A 2% yield would result from dividing $2 by $100, but this stock costs $50, so the yield is higher than 2%.
ww.25%: A 25% yield would need $12.50 in dividends on a $50 stock, but the stock pays only $2 a year, so the yield is far lower.
ww.52%: A 52% result comes from adding $2 and $50, but yield requires dividing dividends by price, not adding them, so 52% is incorrect.

rw: Debt-to-equity is total liabilities divided by shareholders' equity, showing how much a company relies on borrowed money compared with owner funds.

ww.Net income divided by total sales: Net income divided by total sales is the net profit margin, which measures profitability, not leverage, so it is not debt-to-equity.
ww.Assets divided by sales for the year: Assets divided by sales is related to asset turnover in inverted form, a measure of efficiency, and not the debt-to-equity leverage ratio.
ww.Share price divided by the earnings: Share price divided by earnings is the P/E ratio, a valuation measure, and it says nothing about how much debt a company carries.

rw: ROE measures net income relative to shareholders' equity, showing how effectively a company turns the owners' invested money into profit for the year.

ww.The tax rate a company pays to the state: The tax rate a company pays is an effective tax rate, which is unrelated to ROE, a profitability measure using net income and equity.
ww.The interest rate on a loan to a company: The interest rate on a loan is the cost of borrowing, not ROE, which measures the profit a company earns on shareholders' money.
ww.The growth in the number of shares owned: Growth in the number of shares owned is share count change or dilution, not ROE, which measures profit relative to shareholders' equity.

rw: A current ratio below 1 means short-term liabilities exceed short-term assets, so the company may struggle to pay its debts due within a year.

ww.A company has far too much spare cash: A current ratio below 1 means current liabilities exceed current assets, which signals a shortage of liquid resources and not too much spare cash.
ww.A company is very profitable with cash: A weak current ratio indicates liquidity strain rather than strong profitability, and profit and liquidity are different things, so this does not follow.
ww.A company has no debt at all to pay: A company with no debt to pay would have no current liabilities and a very high current ratio, not one below 1.

rw: Book value per share is shareholders' equity divided by shares outstanding, showing the accounting value of the company that belongs to each share.

ww.The dividends paid per share each year t: Dividends paid per share each year is the dividend per share figure, not book value per share, which relates equity to the share count.
ww.The target price set by analysts for the: An analyst's target price is a forecast of future market value, whereas book value per share comes from the balance sheet equity.
ww.The price at which a share last traded o: The last traded price is the market price, which reflects investor expectations, and may differ widely from the accounting book value per share.

rw: Trading far below book value may mean the market sees the stock as undervalued, or that it sees serious problems, such as poor earnings or asset quality.

ww.The company cannot be sold to anyone at: A low price relative to book value does not stop a sale; shares still trade, and the company can still be bought or sold.
ww.The company has no assets left to sell a: Trading below book value does not mean no assets remain; book value is based on assets minus liabilities, so there are still recorded assets.
ww.The stock is certain to rise toward its: A discount to book value does not guarantee any rise; the market may be correctly pricing problems, so the word "certain" makes this wrong.

rw: Beta measures a stock's volatility compared with the overall market, so a beta above 1 means the stock tends to swing more than the market.

ww.A measure of dividends a company pays to: Dividends paid are measured by dividend yield or payout ratio, not beta, which captures how a stock moves in relation to the market.
ww.A measure of a company's total debt load: Total debt is measured by ratios such as debt to equity, not beta, which is concerned with price sensitivity to market movements.
ww.A measure of a company's age and size in: Age and size of a company are not captured by beta, which is a statistical measure of price movement relative to the market.

rw: A beta of 1.5 means the stock tends to move about 50% more than the market, so a 10% market rise suggests about 15% for the stock.

ww.It always matches the market exactly eac: A beta of 1.5 means the stock is more volatile than the market, so it does not match the market exactly each day.
ww.It moves 50% less than the market overal: A beta of 0.5 would mean moving 50% less than the market, but 1.5 is above 1, so it means moving more.
ww.It never moves up or down in price at al: A stock that never moves would have a beta near zero, but 1.5 means it is more volatile than the market, not static.

rw: Standard deviation measures how widely returns vary around their average, so it is used as a gauge of an investment's volatility and risk.

ww.Measuring a company's total dividends: Total dividends are measured by adding up payments per share, not by standard deviation, which measures how much returns spread around their average.
ww.Measuring the number of shares: The number of shares is simply a count from the company's records, and standard deviation is a statistical measure of spread, not a count.
ww.Measuring the tax owed on all gains: Tax owed on gains is calculated from tax rules and the amount of gain, not standard deviation, which measures return variability.

rw: A 52-week high is the highest price at which a stock traded during the past year, and investors use it as a reference for how strong a stock has been.

ww.The price on the first trading day of th: The price on the first trading day of the year is an opening reference, not a 52-week high, which is the highest price over the last year.
ww.The lowest price at which a stock traded: The lowest price during the past year is the 52-week low, the opposite of the 52-week high, which marks the highest trading price in that period.
ww.The target price set by an analyst for t: An analyst's target price is a forecast for the future, while a 52-week high is a historical record of the highest trading price in the past year.

rw: A moving average is the average price over a recent number of periods, updated as new data arrives, and it smooths out short-term price swings.

ww.The percent of profit paid as dividends: The percent of profit paid as dividends is the payout ratio, not a moving average, which smooths price data over recent periods.
ww.The price at which a stock opens each da: The opening price is just where the first trade of the day occurs, while a moving average calculates the mean of prices across many recent periods.
ww.The total number of shares traded: The total number of shares traded is trading volume, not a moving average, which averages prices rather than counting how many shares changed hands.

rw: Support is a price level where a stock has tended to stop falling, because buyers step in there and demand halts further decline in the price.

ww.A price level where a stock tends to sto: A level where a stock tends to stop rising is resistance, not support, because support describes the price floor where falling prices have tended to stop.
ww.The price set by regulators for the stoc: Regulators do not set a daily price for stocks; support is a technical idea from past trading behavior and not a price set by authorities.
ww.The price paid by the company's founders: The price paid by founders is an early cost basis and has no connection to support, which is a chart level where price tended to stop falling.

rw: Resistance is a price level where a stock has tended to stop rising, because sellers appear there and supply caps further upward moves in price.

ww.A price level set by analysts for the st: Analysts publish price targets, which are forecasts, but resistance is a chart level formed by past trading and not set by analysts each year.
ww.A price level where a stock tends to sto: A level where a stock tends to stop falling is support, not resistance, because support acts as a price floor where buyers step in.
ww.A price level that is illegal to cross f: Nothing makes crossing a price level illegal; stocks can trade through resistance, and traders often take a breakout above resistance as a bullish sign.

rw: A fundamental analyst studies financial reports such as quarterly earnings and balance sheets to estimate a company's true value and judge whether the stock is priced fairly.

ww.A technical analyst: A technical analyst studies price charts and trading volume to forecast moves, rather than examining quarterly earnings reports and balance sheets to value a company.
ww.A chart reader only: A chart reader only looks at price patterns and does not study financial statements, so this person would not examine earnings and balance sheets to value stock.
ww.A weather forecaster: A weather forecaster predicts weather, not company value, so this person would have no reason to study earnings reports and balance sheets for valuing stock.

rw: A technical analyst relies on chart patterns and trading volume to spot trends and forecast price moves, instead of studying a company's financial statements.

ww.A fundamental analyst: A fundamental analyst studies financial statements and business value rather than relying mainly on chart patterns and trading volume to forecast prices.
ww.A tax return preparer: A tax return preparer completes tax filings for clients and does not analyze price charts or trading volume to forecast stock price movements.
ww.A company auditor: A company auditor checks financial statements for accuracy and compliance, and does not use chart patterns or trading volume to predict stock prices.

rw: An analyst's price target is a forecast of where the analyst expects a stock's price to be in the future, usually over the next twelve months.

ww.The price at which a stock must be sold: No law forces a stock to be sold at a given price; a price target is an opinion, not a legal sale requirement.
ww.The price paid by the company's board of: A board of directors does not pay a price target; it is only an analyst's estimate and is not a transaction price.
ww.The fee charged for analysis of the stoc: Fees charged for analysis are research costs and have no connection to a price target, which is a forecast of a future stock price.

rw: A prospectus is a legal document describing a security offering, including the issuer's business, finances and risks, so buyers can make informed decisions.

ww.A tax form for investors who hold stock: A tax form for investors holding stock is not a prospectus; a prospectus is an offering document describing a security and its risks to buyers.
ww.A newspaper stock table with prices of t: A newspaper stock table shows daily prices, whereas a prospectus is a legal document that describes the security being offered and the issuing company.
ww.A list of the broker's fees only, no com: A prospectus contains extensive company data, such as financials and risk factors, rather than just a list of broker fees, so this option is wrong.

rw: A 10-K is the annual report public companies file with the SEC, containing audited financial statements and a full description of the business and its risks.

ww.A tax return for corporations and firms: A corporate tax return is filed with the IRS, not the SEC, and the 10-K is instead a detailed annual disclosure of the business.
ww.A quarterly report filed with the SEC: A quarterly report filed with the SEC is the 10-Q, which covers only three months, while the 10-K covers the full fiscal year.
ww.A report about an unusual event: A report about an unusual event describes an 8-K, which companies file for significant events, and not the annual 10-K report.

rw: A 10-Q is the quarterly report public companies file with the SEC, containing unaudited financial statements and updates on the business for the quarter just ended.

ww.A prospectus for new shares of stock: A prospectus is the document for a new securities offering, but a 10-Q is a routine periodic report filed after each of the first three quarters.
ww.A report on major events between quarter: A report on major events between quarters is the 8-K, not the 10-Q, which is the regular quarterly financial report.
ww.An annual report filed with the SEC: An annual report filed with the SEC is the 10-K, which covers the full year, while the 10-Q covers only a single quarter.

rw: The SEC's EDGAR database is a free public system where investors can search and read filings such as 10-Ks, 10-Qs and 8-Ks.

ww.A broker's private chat room: A broker's private chat room is not a public source of filings; it is restricted to clients and does not hold official company reports.
ww.The IRS tax portal site: The IRS tax portal handles tax matters for taxpayers and does not hold public companies' securities filings, which are kept by the SEC.
ww.The FDIC website for banks: The FDIC website concerns deposit insurance and bank information, not securities filings, which public companies submit to the SEC and publish on EDGAR.

rw: A security is a financial instrument, such as a stock or bond, showing ownership or debt rights, and can be traded in financial markets.

ww.A promise made by a friend to repay a lo: A friend's promise to repay a loan is a personal informal arrangement and is not a standardized, tradable financial instrument like a security.
ww.A password used to log in to an account: A password protects account access and is a different meaning of the word "security", not the financial instrument that represents ownership or debt.
ww.A guard hired to protect a bank vault at: A guard protecting a vault is a security guard, a different sense of the word, and is not the financial instrument investors buy and sell.

rw: Common stock represents ownership in a company and usually carries voting rights, with dividends that vary depending on the company's profits and board decisions.

ww.A deposit with a bank that earns a fixed: A deposit earning fixed interest at a bank is a savings product, not common stock, which represents ownership in a company with variable dividends.
ww.A loan made to a company that must be re: A loan to a company repaid with interest by a set date is a bond, which is debt, whereas common stock is an ownership share.
ww.Ownership shares with a fixed dividend a: Fixed dividends with no vote describe features of some preferred stock, while common stock usually carries voting rights and dividends that can change.

rw: Preferred stock pays a fixed dividend and has priority over common stock for dividend payments and for claims on assets if the company liquidates.

ww.Stock that is given free to employees as: Stock given free to employees as pay is employee stock compensation, which can be common stock, so it does not define preferred stock.
ww.Stock with unlimited voting rights and d: Unlimited voting rights with variable dividends and no priority describe common stock, which is the opposite of preferred stock with its payment priority.
ww.Stock that pays no dividend ever and has: Preferred stock normally does pay a dividend and does have a claim on assets ahead of common holders, so this description is inaccurate.

rw: Creditors and bondholders hold legal claims for money owed, so they are paid first in liquidation, before preferred and then common stockholders receive anything.

ww.Common stockholders first: Common stockholders are paid last in liquidation, after creditors and preferred holders, since they own the residual value left after all claims are satisfied.
ww.The company's customers: Customers are not first in line for liquidation proceeds; creditors with legal claims, such as lenders and bondholders, get paid before owners.
ww.Preferred stockholders: Preferred stockholders are paid after creditors and bondholders, though ahead of common stockholders, so they are not the first group paid in liquidation.

rw: A corporate bond is a loan to a company in return for interest, with the principal repaid at maturity, making the buyer a creditor.

ww.A type of insurance policy sold to firms: An insurance policy sold to firms is a risk transfer contract, not a bond, which is a tradable loan from investors to a company.
ww.A government savings account for firms: Government savings accounts are not corporate bonds; a corporate bond is issued by a private company to borrow money from investors.
ww.A share of ownership held by investors: A share of ownership is stock, not a bond; a bondholder is a lender to the company and does not own part of it.

rw: The coupon rate is the yearly interest rate on the bond's face value, so it fixes the dollar amount of interest paid each year.

ww.The price paid for the bond by investors: The price paid by investors is the market price, which can differ from face value, while the coupon rate is a percent of face value.
ww.The date the bond is repaid in full: The date a bond is repaid in full is the maturity date, which is a separate feature from the coupon rate of interest.
ww.The tax rate on the bond interest paid: The tax rate on bond interest is set by tax law for the investor, while the coupon rate is the interest rate the issuer pays.

rw: Annual interest equals the coupon rate times face value, so 5% of $1,000 is $50, which the bond pays each year to the holder.

ww.$5: Paying only $5 would equal 0.5% of face value, but a 5% coupon on $1,000 produces ten times that amount each year.
ww.$1,050: A payment of $1,050 would add the interest to the face value, but yearly interest is only 5% of $1,000, not the total.
ww.$500: A payment of $500 would be 50% of face value, but a 5% coupon pays $50 each year on a $1,000 bond.

rw: Face (par) value is the amount the issuer repays to the bondholder at maturity, and it is also the base on which coupon interest is calculated.

ww.The fee paid to a broker for buying the: A fee paid to a broker is a transaction cost, whereas face value is the amount the issuer repays the bondholder when the bond matures.
ww.The interest paid each year on the bond: The interest paid each year is the coupon payment, calculated from the coupon rate, and is not the face or par value of the bond.
ww.The price a bond sells for each day in t: The price a bond sells for each day is its market price, which can be above or below its par value as interest rates change.

rw: A bond priced at $950 is below its $1,000 face value, so it is described as trading at a discount to par value.

ww.Trading at a premium: Trading at a premium means the price is above face value, but $950 is below the $1,000 face value, so the bond is not at a premium.
ww.Trading at maturity: Trading at maturity is not a price description; maturity is the date the bond is repaid, and price versus face value defines discount or premium.
ww.Trading at par value: Trading at par means the price equals the $1,000 face value, but this bond trades at $950, which is $50 below par.

rw: A zero-coupon bond makes no periodic interest payments; it sells at a discount to face value and pays full face value at maturity, which is the investor's return.

ww.A bond that pays interest every single m: Paying interest every month is a feature of a regular income bond, whereas a zero-coupon bond has a coupon rate of zero and pays no interest.
ww.A bond that pays dividends to holders ea: Dividends are paid by stocks, not bonds; a zero-coupon bond pays no periodic payments of any kind and instead earns the gap between price and face value.
ww.A bond that never repays the face value: A zero-coupon bond does repay its face value at maturity; that repayment, bought at a discount, is exactly how the investor earns a return.

rw: A callable bond lets the issuer repay it before maturity, often when interest rates fall so that the issuer can refinance its debt more cheaply.

ww.A bond that cannot be repaid before the: A bond that cannot be repaid early describes a non-callable bond, the opposite of a callable bond, which the issuer has the right to redeem early.
ww.A bond the buyer can convert into stock: A bond the buyer can convert to stock is a convertible bond, which is a different feature from the issuer's right to call it.
ww.A bond traded by phone only, not on an e: Callable has nothing to do with phone trading; bonds trade over the counter or on exchanges, and callable describes the issuer's early redemption right.

rw: A convertible bond gives holders the right to exchange it for a set number of shares of the issuer's stock, adding equity upside to a bond.

ww.A bond that is issued in other currencie: A bond issued in other currencies by foreign firms describes a foreign currency bond, which says nothing about the holder's right to swap it for stock.
ww.A bond that can be turned into cash at a: Turning a bond into cash at any bank on demand is not a feature of convertible bonds; conversion refers to exchanging the bond for shares.
ww.A bond that the issuer may call at any t: A bond the issuer may call at any time is a callable bond, where the issuer holds the right, whereas convertible rights belong to the holder.

rw: A T-bill is a short-term government security, maturing in a year or less, sold at a discount to face value, and the investor earns the difference.

ww.A tax paid to the Treasury by firms each: A tax paid to the Treasury by firms is a corporate tax, not a T-bill, which is a short-term security the government sells to borrow money.
ww.A long-term corporate bond sold by firms: A long-term corporate bond sold by firms is private-sector debt, whereas a T-bill is issued by the government with a maturity of one year or less.
ww.A share of ownership in the Treasury pay: Treasury bills are debt, not ownership shares, and they pay no dividend; investors earn the difference between the discounted purchase price and face value.

rw: A Treasury note is a U.S. government security that matures in two to ten years and pays interest every six months until it matures.

ww.A corporate note issued by a private fir: A corporate note issued by a private firm is not a Treasury note, because Treasury notes are issued by the U.S. government, not by companies.
ww.A thirty-year government bond paying int: A thirty-year government bond is a Treasury bond, which has a much longer maturity than a Treasury note, which runs two to ten years.
ww.A one-month government loan paid back to: A one-month government loan is a short-term Treasury bill, since notes have much longer maturities than one month, running from two years up to ten.

rw: Treasury securities are backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government, which has the power to tax and borrow, so default risk is very low.

ww.They are insured by a private company th: Treasuries are not insured by a private company; their safety comes from the government's ability to repay, not from any private insurance payout.
ww.They are issued by banks and private cre: Treasuries are issued by the U.S. government through the Treasury Department, not by banks or credit unions, so that statement is wrong about the issuer.
ww.They always rise in price every year for: Treasury prices fall as well as rise when interest rates change, so they do not always rise every year; their low risk refers to default.

rw: A savings bond is low-risk government debt designed for individual savers, who lend money to the government and receive interest over time.

ww.A corporate loan from a bank to a firm: A corporate loan from a bank to a firm is private lending, but a savings bond is government debt that an individual buys.
ww.A bank deposit that is insured by the FD: A bank deposit insured by the FDIC is a deposit account, not a savings bond, which is a debt security issued by the government.
ww.A stock issued by a savings bank to save: A savings bond is debt, not stock, and it is issued by the U.S. government rather than by any savings bank to its savers.

rw: NAV is the value of the fund's holdings minus its debts, divided by shares, which gives the per-share value at which fund shares are priced.

ww.The fund's yearly return to investors: The fund's yearly return measures performance, not NAV, which is a per-share value of assets less liabilities at a point in time.
ww.The number of investors who own shares: The number of investors is a count of shareholders and says nothing about the per-share value of the fund's net assets.
ww.The fee paid to the fund manager each ye: The fee paid to the fund manager is the management fee or expense ratio, which is separate from NAV, the net asset value per share.

rw: NAV equals assets minus liabilities divided by shares, so $50 million minus $2 million is $48 million, divided by 4 million shares gives $12.00.

ww.$13.00: An NAV of $13.00 would come from dividing $52 million by 4 million shares, but net assets are $48 million after subtracting liabilities, so it is too high.
ww.$12.50: An NAV of $12.50 divides the $50 million assets by 4 million shares, ignoring the $2 million of liabilities that must be subtracted first.
ww.$1.20: An NAV of $1.20 puts the decimal in the wrong place; $48 million divided by 4 million shares gives $12.00, not $1.20.

rw: A load is a sales charge on mutual fund shares, paid when buying (front-end) or selling (back-end), which compensates brokers who sell the fund.

ww.The fund's interest rate paid: The interest rate a fund pays is not a load; a load is a sales charge paid by the investor when buying or selling fund shares.
ww.The fund's yearly dividend: A fund's yearly dividend is a distribution to shareholders, not a load, which is a fee that goes to compensate the sales channel.
ww.The weight of the fund's holdings: The weight of a fund's holdings refers to the proportion of each investment in the portfolio, whereas a load is a sales charge on shares.

rw: ETFs trade on an exchange throughout the day at changing prices, while traditional mutual funds are priced once daily after the market closes at NAV.

ww.ETFs cannot be bought by individual peop: ETFs can be bought by individuals through a brokerage account, so saying they cannot be bought by individual people is false.
ww.Mutual funds trade throughout the day li: Mutual funds do not trade all day like stocks; they price once daily, while ETFs are the funds that trade throughout the trading day.
ww.ETFs never hold stocks or bonds in them: ETFs hold stocks, bonds or other assets in their portfolios, just as mutual funds do, so saying they hold none is incorrect.

rw: In an actively managed fund, a manager picks investments and trades them in an attempt to beat the market or a benchmark index.

ww.A fund that has no manager to run its pi: An actively managed fund does have a manager who selects its investments, so a fund with no manager describes an automated structure, not active management.
ww.A fund that holds only cash and short bo: Holding only cash and short bonds describes a type of money market or short-term fund, and it does not define active management.
ww.A fund that tracks an index and is rarel: A fund that tracks an index and is rarely changed is passively managed, which is the opposite of an actively managed fund.

rw: A passively managed fund tracks a market index with little trading, so it keeps costs low and aims to match the market's return.

ww.A fund in which a manager trades often t: A manager who trades often to beat the market describes an actively managed fund, which is the opposite of a passive approach.
ww.A fund that never changes its holdings a: Passive funds do change holdings when the index changes or when investors add money, so saying they never change anything at all is wrong.
ww.A fund that holds one stock only at a ti: A fund holding one stock at a time is highly concentrated, while a passive fund holds the many securities of the index it tracks.

rw: A money market fund invests in short-term, high-quality debt, such as T-bills and commercial paper, and aims to keep a stable share value.

ww.A bank savings account that is insured b: A bank savings account insured by the FDIC is a bank deposit, whereas a money market fund is an investment fund not insured by the FDIC.
ww.A fund that buys real estate and land fo: A fund buying real estate and land for rent describes a real estate investment, not a money market fund, which holds short-term debt.
ww.A fund that invests only in risky penny: Money market funds hold safe short-term debt and are conservative, so a fund investing only in risky penny stocks is the opposite of one.

rw: A call option gives the holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy an asset at a set strike price by a specified date.

ww.A stock that pays calls to investors: A call option is a contract, not a stock, and it does not pay calls to investors; it grants a right to buy.
ww.A contract giving the right to sell an a: A contract giving the right to sell an asset is a put option, not a call, which gives the holder the right to buy.
ww.A contract requiring the holder to buy: A contract requiring the holder to buy describes an obligation, but a call option gives a right, not an obligation, so the holder may decline.

rw: A put option gives the holder the right, but not the obligation, to sell an asset at a set strike price by a given date.

ww.A stock that pays dividends to holders: A put option is a derivative contract, not a stock, and it does not pay dividends; it gives the holder the right to sell.
ww.A contract to sell a stock at a set pric: A contract to sell a stock at a set price describes an obligation, but a put option gives the holder a right, not a duty.
ww.A contract giving the right to buy share: A contract giving the right to buy shares is a call option, whereas a put option instead gives the right to sell.

rw: The strike price is the fixed price at which the holder of an option may buy (call) or sell (put) the underlying asset.

ww.The tax on the option contract itself: A tax on the contract is not a strike price; the strike price is set in the option contract and fixes the price for exercising.
ww.The price at which the stock opened on t: The price at which the stock opened on the day is an opening price, which is unrelated to the strike price written in the contract.
ww.The price of the option contract itself: The price of the option contract itself is the premium, while the strike price is the fixed exercise price of the underlying asset.

rw: The premium is the price paid by the buyer to the seller to purchase an option contract, and it is the buyer's maximum possible loss.

ww.The dividend paid on a stock each year: A dividend on a stock is a distribution paid to shareholders, not an option premium, which is the cost of buying the option contract.
ww.The price at which the stock is exercise: The price at which the stock is exercised is the strike price, whereas the premium is the amount paid to buy the option itself.
ww.The commission paid to a broker for a tr: A commission paid to a broker is a trading fee, which is separate from the option premium that the buyer pays to the seller.

rw: The call is worth $10 at exercise because $60 minus the $50 strike is $10, and subtracting the $2 premium gives a profit of $8 per share.

ww.$10: A $10 profit ignores the cost of the option; the stock rose $10 above the strike, but the $2 premium paid must be subtracted.
ww.$12: A $12 profit adds the premium to the gain, but the premium is a cost paid by the buyer, so it must be subtracted instead.
ww.$2: A $2 profit confuses profit with the premium; the premium is the cost, and the call's $10 gain less $2 leaves $8 per share.

rw: A $40 strike put is worthless when the stock is at $45 because selling at $40 is worse than the market, so the investor loses the $3 premium.

ww.The investor is forced to buy the stock: A put holder is never forced to buy the stock; a put gives the right to sell, and the holder simply lets it lapse when not useful.
ww.The investor earns $3 per share in profi: Earning $3 per share is wrong because $3 is the premium the buyer paid, and with the stock above the strike the put has no value.
ww.The investor earns $5 per share in profi: A $5 profit would be the gap between $45 and $40, but that gap works against a put holder, as it is worth nothing, so profit is not made.

rw: A warrant is a long-term right, issued by a company, to buy its stock at a set price, and it often lasts for years.

ww.A dividend payment made to holders: A dividend payment made to holders is a distribution of profits, whereas a warrant is a long-term right to buy company stock at a set price.
ww.A court order to arrest an investor over: A court order to arrest someone is a legal warrant, a different meaning of the word from the financial instrument that gives rights to buy stock.
ww.A short-term bank loan to a company: A short-term bank loan to a company is a debt, whereas a warrant is not a loan but a right to buy shares directly from the issuer.

rw: A stock dividend is a distribution of extra shares to existing shareholders instead of cash, which increases the number of shares each holder owns.

ww.A tax on holding stock shares: A stock dividend is a payment to shareholders, not a tax; taxes on stock holding are levied by governments and not by the company.
ww.A fee for owning stock shares: A stock dividend is a benefit for shareholders and not a fee; owning stock may involve fees to brokers, but those are not dividends.
ww.A cash payment from a bank yearly: A stock dividend comes from the issuing company and not from a bank, and it pays out extra shares rather than a cash payment.

rw: An ADR is a certificate issued by a U.S. bank representing shares of a foreign company, letting U.S. investors trade them on U.S. exchanges in dollars.

ww.A U.S. savings bond sold to ordinary U.S: A U.S. savings bond is government debt for domestic savers, whereas an ADR is a certificate representing shares of a foreign company traded in the U.S.
ww.A bank loan to a foreign firm made by a: A bank loan to a foreign firm is credit, not an ownership certificate, so it differs from an ADR, which represents foreign company shares.
ww.A tax form for foreign income earned by: A tax form for foreign income is a reporting document, and an ADR is not a form but a security that investors buy and sell.

rw: A structured product is a packaged investment, often combining bonds and derivatives, whose payoff follows set rules tied to an index or asset.

ww.A free government giveaway to citizens: A free government giveaway to citizens is a benefit program, not an investment, whereas a structured product is a packaged investment with preset payoff rules.
ww.A building purchased as an investment fo: A building purchased as an investment for rent is direct real estate, not a structured product, which is a packaged security built from other instruments.
ww.A simple savings account at a local bank: A simple savings account at a local bank is a basic deposit product, whereas a structured product is a complex packaged security with set payoff rules.

rw: A CD is a deposit insured by the FDIC up to legal limits and held to term, while a bond is tradable debt sold by an issuer.

ww.A CD is a share of stock in a company's: A CD is a bank deposit, not stock, so it gives no share of ownership in a company's equity, unlike shares.
ww.A CD always pays more than a bond, as ba: A CD does not always pay more than a bond; bonds can have higher yields, and bank backing does not guarantee a higher rate.
ww.A CD cannot earn any interest at all in: A CD does earn interest during its term, which is the whole purpose of the product, so saying it cannot earn any is false.

rw: In a limited partnership, limited partners supply capital and have limited liability, while a general partner runs the business and bears full responsibility for its debts.

ww.An investment where all partners share u: In a limited partnership, limited partners have liability limited to their investment, and only the general partner has unlimited liability, so not all partners share unlimited risk.
ww.An investment guaranteed by the governme: Limited partnerships carry no government guarantee; investors can lose money, and a state's backing does not apply to this private business structure.
ww.An investment in a savings account at a: A savings account at a local bank is a deposit product, not a partnership investment in which limited partners fund a business run by a general partner.

rw: A UIT holds a fixed portfolio that is not actively traded and ends on a stated termination date, when proceeds go back to investors.

ww.A stock exchange for trading company sha: A stock exchange is a marketplace where shares trade, whereas a unit investment trust is a fund with a fixed portfolio.
ww.A bank account with a fixed rate of inte: A bank account with a fixed rate of interest is a deposit, while a UIT holds a set portfolio of securities for investors.
ww.A fund that trades often to follow the m: A fund that trades often to follow the market describes active management, while a UIT keeps its portfolio fixed until it ends.

rw: A closed-end fund issues a fixed number of shares at launch, and those shares then trade on an exchange like a stock, at market-set prices.

ww.A fund that continually issues new share: A fund that continually issues new shares and redeems old ones at NAV is an open-end mutual fund, not a closed-end fund.
ww.A fund that is closed to all new investo: Closed-end funds are not closed to all investors or impossible to sell; their shares trade freely on an exchange between buyers and sellers.
ww.A fund that holds only cash and short-te: Holding only cash and short-term bills describes a money market fund and not a closed-end fund, which is defined by its fixed share count.

rw: An open-end mutual fund continually issues new shares and redeems existing ones at net asset value, so the number of shares changes with investor demand.

ww.A fund with a fixed number of exchange-t: A fixed number of exchange-traded shares describes a closed-end fund, not an open-end fund, whose share count grows and shrinks with purchases and redemptions.
ww.A fund that never changes its mix of hol: Open-end funds do change holdings as managers buy and sell investments, and the phrase open-end refers to share issuance, not to unchanging holdings.
ww.A fund that is open only to employees of: Open-end funds are sold to the general public and not only to employees of one firm, so that description does not define one.

rw: Because a closed-end fund has a fixed share count and trades on an exchange, supply and demand set its price, which can sit below NAV.

ww.The fund manager sets the price daily: Closed-end fund shares trade on an exchange, so the market sets the price during the day, not a manager who sets the price daily.
ww.The fund is not allowed to hold securiti: Closed-end funds are allowed to hold securities, which is their whole purpose, so the discount cannot come from a ban on holding them.
ww.The government sets the discount by law: No law sets the discount; closed-end fund prices come from market trading, so the government does not fix them at a discount.

rw: A target-date fund automatically shifts its mix from stocks toward bonds as the chosen retirement date approaches, lowering risk as the investor gets closer to retiring.

ww.A fund that never changes its holdings a: A target-date fund does change its holdings over time, so saying that it never changes and keeps the same mix describes a static fund, not it.
ww.A fund that pays out all its assets to i: A target-date fund does not pay out all assets on a single date and close; it keeps investing, and it shifts to a safer mix as the date nears.
ww.A fund that invests only in one company: A target-date fund is diversified across many securities and not a single company, so a fund holding only one company fails to describe it.

rw: A balanced fund holds a set mix of stocks and bonds, such as 60 percent stocks and 40 percent bonds, to balance growth and income.

ww.A fund holding only stocks and no bonds: A fund holding only stocks and no bonds is an equity fund, not a balanced fund, which blends stocks with bonds.
ww.A fund holding only cash and no stocks a: A fund holding only cash and no stocks is a cash or money market fund, not a balanced fund, which holds both stocks and bonds.
ww.A fund balanced by order of the governme: A balanced fund is balanced by its own mix of asset types and not by any order of the government, so this is wrong.

rw: A sector fund invests in a single industry, such as technology or health care, so its results depend heavily on how that industry performs.

ww.A fund that invests across all industrie: A fund spreading across all industries equally is a broad diversified fund, while a sector fund concentrates on a single industry.
ww.A fund that lends money to farmers and g: A fund that lends money to farmers is an agricultural lending vehicle, not a sector fund, which holds shares of companies within one industry.
ww.A fund that invests in government bonds: A fund investing only in government bonds is a bond fund by asset type, not a sector fund, which is defined by industry focus.

rw: A sector fund focused on one industry lacks diversification, so its value swings more widely with that industry's fortunes and is likely to be more volatile.

ww.A short-term Treasury bill fund at a ban: A short-term Treasury bill fund holds very short maturities of government debt, which are stable in price, so it is among the least volatile funds.
ww.A money market fund for cash savers: A money market fund aims to hold a stable share value by investing in short-term safe debt, so it is much less volatile.
ww.A broad index fund of hundreds of firms: A broad index fund holds hundreds of firms across industries, which spreads risk, so it is less volatile than a fund concentrated in a single sector.

rw: An international fund invests in companies located outside the investor's home country, giving access to foreign markets and diversification beyond domestic stocks and bonds.

ww.A fund that pays in foreign currency onl: An international fund does not just pay in foreign currency; the key feature is that it invests in companies outside the investor's home country.
ww.A fund that lends money to foreign gover: Lending money to foreign governments at a low rate is a narrow bond strategy, not the general definition of an international fund.
ww.A fund that invests only in U.S. compani: A fund investing only in U.S. companies and U.S. bonds is a domestic fund, the opposite of an international fund for investors.

rw: Currency risk is the chance that exchange rate changes reduce the value of foreign holdings when converted back to the investor's home currency.

ww.The risk that interest rates fall in the: Falling interest rates describe interest rate risk, not currency risk, which concerns changes in exchange rates affecting the value of foreign investments.
ww.The risk that a company stops paying div: A company ceasing to pay dividends is a business or dividend risk, not currency risk, which comes from changes in exchange rates.
ww.The risk that a stock exchange closes do: A stock exchange closing for a day is an operational or market risk, whereas currency risk comes from movements in exchange rates.

rw: A rights offering gives current shareholders the right to buy new shares, often at a discount, usually in proportion to the shares they already hold.

ww.An offer to refund fees to investors who: An offer to refund fees to investors is a fee rebate, not a rights offering, which gives shareholders the chance to buy new shares.
ww.An offer to give away free stock to the: A rights offering is not a free giveaway to the public; existing shareholders get the right to buy new shares, usually at a discount.
ww.An offer to sell the firm to a rival for: Selling the firm to a rival is a merger or acquisition and not a rights offering, which raises capital by issuing new shares.

rw: Dilution means existing holders' ownership percentage shrinks when a company issues more shares, so each existing share represents a smaller slice of the company.

ww.An increase in the value of each share h: An increase in the value of each share is the opposite of dilution, which reduces each holder's percentage ownership and may reduce earnings per share.
ww.A rise in dividends paid to all holders: A rise in dividends paid to all holders is a payout increase, not dilution, which refers to a shrinking ownership share after new shares are issued.
ww.A tax on large holdings of stock by firm: A tax on large holdings is a government levy and not dilution, which is a drop in ownership percentage from the issue of new shares.

rw: In a stock buyback, a company repurchases its own shares from the market, reducing shares outstanding and often returning cash to shareholders in place of dividends.

ww.An investor returning shares to the firm: An investor returning shares to the firm for a refund is not how a buyback works; the company buys shares from holders on the market.
ww.A company issuing more shares to the pub: A company issuing more shares for cash is the opposite of a buyback, which reduces the number of shares outstanding instead of adding to it.
ww.A broker repurchasing a client's account: A broker repurchasing a client's account for a fee is a brokerage service and not a buyback, which a company does with its own shares.

rw: A buyback tends to raise EPS because earnings are divided among fewer shares outstanding, so each remaining share gets a larger portion of net income.

ww.It tends to decrease EPS: A buyback reduces the share count in the EPS denominator, so EPS tends to increase rather than decrease, other things being equal.
ww.It has no effect on EPS: Because a buyback shrinks the number of shares, the EPS calculation changes, so saying it has no effect on EPS is incorrect.
ww.It cancels all earnings: A buyback does not cancel earnings; the company still earns profit, and only the number of shares used to divide those earnings falls.

rw: A mortgage-backed security is backed by a pool of home loans, and investors receive payments from the principal and interest paid by the borrowers.

ww.A tax break for homeowners with loans: A tax break for homeowners is a deduction, not an investment product, whereas a mortgage-backed security is backed by a pool of home loans.
ww.A stock issued by a home builder firm: A stock issued by a home builder is equity in a construction company, not a mortgage-backed security, which is backed by loans.
ww.A savings account for first-time home bu: A savings account for first-time home buyers is a bank deposit product, not a security backed by a pool of mortgage loans.

rw: Securitization pools loans, such as mortgages, and sells securities whose payments come from the cash flows of those loans, spreading risk among investors.

ww.Keeping assets in a vault for safekeepin: Keeping assets in a vault is physical safekeeping, which is a different meaning from securitization, which turns loans into tradable securities.
ww.Insuring a house against fire damage and: Insuring a house against fire is property insurance, which has nothing to do with securitization, which bundles loans into securities for sale.
ww.Hiring guards to protect assets, such as: Hiring guards to protect assets is physical security, a different meaning of the word, and it is not securitization of loans.

rw: A broker-dealer acts as a broker when trading for clients and as a dealer when trading for its own account, so it does both.

ww.A firm that only lends to homebuyers: A firm that only lends to homebuyers is a mortgage lender, but a broker-dealer works in securities, buying and selling for clients and itself.
ww.A firm that only sells insurance policie: A firm that only sells insurance policies is an insurance agency, whereas a broker-dealer trades securities as an agent and as a principal.
ww.A firm that only prints money for the st: Printing money is done by government mints and printing bureaus, not by a broker-dealer, which is a securities firm acting for clients and itself.

rw: The SEC regulates securities markets to protect investors, enforces disclosure and anti-fraud rules, and oversees exchanges, brokers and public company reporting in the United States.

ww.Collects income taxes from the public: Collecting income taxes is the job of the Internal Revenue Service, not the SEC, which focuses on securities markets and investor protection.
ww.Insures bank deposits up to a legal limi: Insuring bank deposits up to a legal limit is the role of the FDIC, not the SEC, which oversees securities markets and firms.
ww.Sets the federal funds rate for banks: Setting the federal funds rate is done by the Federal Reserve's Open Market Committee, not the SEC, which regulates securities markets instead.
